analysis.one_liner: Requires regular government inspections of food processors, mandatory recall authority for contaminated food, and safety rules for imported food.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee in May 2005 and never advanced further, dying without a vote, a hearing, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Health and Human Services to build a national food safety program for FDA-regulated foods: registering food facilities, inspecting them at least quarterly (with waivers for low-risk plants), setting limits on contaminants like bacteria and toxins, enforcing sanitary processing controls, and checking imported food at ports and in exporting countries. It would have given the government the power to order a stop to distribution of suspected contaminated food and force recalls, impose fines of up to $100,000 per violation per day, protect whistleblowers who report violations, and let citizens sue to enforce safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats FDA-regulated food — essentially all consumers of packaged and processed foods, plus imported foods. The bill targeted the main causes of foodborne illness: pathogens and contaminants in processing plants, and under-inspected imports. People made sick by contaminated food would benefit from faster recalls and consumer notification, and food workers who report unsafe practices would gain legal protection from retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of processed and imported food

how_it_helps.text: Required quarterly, often unannounced, inspections of food processing and importing facilities, with the ability to detain and condemn unsafe food found on site [S3].

Gave the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to order companies to stop distributing contaminated food and to mandate recalls, with consumer notification — authority the FDA generally lacked at the time [S3].

Set health-based limits on contaminants such as bacteria, chemical contaminants, natural toxins, and parasites, with standards protecting sensitive groups like children, the elderly, pregnant women, and the immune-compromised [S3].
Established a system to verify the safety of imported food, including inspections in exporting countries and certification of nations whose food safety systems meet U.S. standards [S3].
Protected employees from being fired or discriminated against for reporting food safety violations or refusing to break the law, and allowed citizens to sue to enforce safety rules [S3].
Required annual facility registration, recordkeeping, and processing controls that companies would have to prove are working through sampling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food processors, manufacturers, warehouses, and importers, who would bear the cost of registering, opening their plants and records to quarterly inspections, installing sanitary processing controls, keeping compliance records, and paying fines of up to $100,000 per violation per day. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on to consumers in food prices, and taxpayers would fund the expanded inspection and surveillance system.

drawbacks.text: Quarterly inspections of every registered facility would be a large and expensive undertaking for the government, and the bill simply authorized 'such sums as may be necessary' without identifying funding [S3].

Compliance costs for processors — sanitation upgrades, recordkeeping, sampling, and more frequent inspections — could be meaningful, especially for small firms, and would likely reach consumers through food prices [S3].

Critics of such regimes argue that broad new inspection mandates and civil penalties can impose heavy paperwork burdens on small food businesses without proportional safety gains, since the bill allowed waivers only for facilities the Secretary certified as low-risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real public health problem — foodborne illness from contaminated processing and weakly inspected imports — and its core tools (mandatory recall authority, regular inspections, contaminant limits) are the same ones Congress later adopted in substance. The main costs are compliance burdens on food companies and the public expense of running a much larger inspection system, partially passed to consumers. On balance the benefits for consumers outweighed the costs, though the bill gave the Secretary broad discretion and open-ended funding rather than a tightly specified program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee in May 2005, and nothing ever happened after that — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors — before the Congress ended in early 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on May 10, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
On May 23, 2005, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed for the remainder of the 109th Congress with no further action [S5].
The bill never attracted any cosponsors [S4].
No roll-call vote, floor action, or hearing record exists for the bill in the 109th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food processors and importers avoided the cost of quarterly inspections, mandatory recall orders, and fines of up to $100,000 per violation, and consumers gained nothing the bill would have provided. Many of its ideas — mandatory recall authority, facility registration, import verification — were adopted years later in the 2011 Food Safety Modernization Act, so the delay meant years without those protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food processors avoided new inspection costs

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; the only member of Congress attached to it.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for food safety legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and took no further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no party lineup — only a single Democratic sponsor and a committee that never acted [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required facility registration, quarterly unannounced inspections, sanitary process controls, recordkeeping, mandatory recall orders, and fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. Its interest in avoiding those costs ran against the consumer protections the same rules provided.

industries.industry: Food importers and foreign food exporters
industries.note: It would have barred unsafe or mislabeled imports, required port-of-entry inspection, and certified only countries with equivalent food safety systems, with intensified checks for the rest. Complying or losing market access was the direct cost of the safety guarantee consumers received.

They would have had to comply with cease-distribution and notification orders for recalled food, but also benefited when contaminated products were pulled from shelves before reaching their customers.
The bill authorized federal advisory, technical, laboratory, and financial aid to strengthen state food safety programs and allowed cooperative inspection agreements.
